title: How Does Spring Pollen Get Into Your Air Ducts?
h1: How Does Spring Pollen Get Into Your Air Ducts?
description: Spring pollen gets into air ducts through open windows, leaky returns, and the air you track inside. Learn how it builds up and how to cut down on it at home.
quick_answer: Pollen gets into air ducts mostly through the return side of the system. It drifts in through open windows and doors, rides in on clothes, shoes and pets, and gets sucked in through leaky return ducts and gaps in attics, garages and closets. Once inside, the HVAC system pulls it toward the filter, and whatever gets past can settle in the ducts.
body:
Spring in Southern California brings a lot of pollen from trees, grasses and weeds, and windy days can carry it a long way. If allergy symptoms don't let up once you're indoors, the problem may be the air moving through your house, not just what's outside.

How does pollen get inside the house?

Pollen is tiny and light, so it finds plenty of ways in:

  • Open windows and doors. On a nice spring day, airing out the house also lets pollen drift right in.
  • People and pets. Pollen sticks to hair, clothes, shoes and fur, then falls onto floors and furniture.
  • Gaps around the house. Weatherstripping, window frames and gaps around pipes all let outside air in.
  • Return duct leaks. This is the one most people don't think about.

Why do leaky return ducts pull in pollen?

Your HVAC system pulls air back through return grilles to the furnace or air handler. If the return ducts or the cabinet have gaps, the system also sucks in air from wherever those gaps are. In Southern California homes, that's usually the attic, the garage or a hall closet.

Attics are dusty, and the attic vents let outside air and pollen in freely. A leaky return in the attic can pull that air straight into the system. Some of it gets past the filter, especially if the leak is on the far side of the filter, and settles in the ducts or blows into your rooms.

Where does pollen build up in the system?

Most of it ends up on the filter, which is what you want. But pollen and dust also collect in these spots:

  1. Return grilles and the first section of the return duct
  2. The blower wheel, if the filter is loose or bypassed
  3. The indoor coil, where moisture helps it stick
  4. Low spots and bends in supply ducts
  5. Supply registers, where you'll see dust on the grilles

When the system starts up, that buildup can get stirred and pushed back into the house.

How can I keep pollen out of my ducts?

A few changes make a real difference during allergy season:

  • Use a better filter. A pleated filter in the MERV 8 to 13 range catches much more pollen than a cheap fiberglass one. Check with a technician that your system can handle the higher rating.
  • Change filters more often in spring. A loaded filter loses airflow and can let more get through around the edges.
  • Make sure the filter fits. Gaps around the filter let air go around it.
  • Keep windows closed on windy, high-pollen days. Run the system instead.
  • Leave shoes at the door and wash pets and bedding more often.
  • Seal return leaks. Sealing the return side keeps attic and garage air out of the system.

Does duct cleaning help with pollen allergies?

It helps when the ducts actually have buildup. If you see dust on registers, puffs of dust when the system starts or a dirty return duct, cleaning removes that reservoir so it isn't blown around every time the system runs. Cleaning won't stop new pollen from entering, so pair it with good filters and duct sealing.

Our air duct cleaning service uses negative pressure and agitation tools to pull debris out instead of pushing it around. For allergy sufferers, our indoor air quality options like upgraded filtration and air purifiers can help too.

When is the best time to clean ducts for allergy season?

Late winter or early spring, before peak pollen, is a good window. That way the system starts the season clean, and new filters can do their job without extra dust load. If you've had a remodel, smoke exposure or pest activity, don't wait for spring.

Windy stretches deserve extra attention. Gusty spring days and Santa Ana winds in the fall push dust and pollen into every gap in the house at once. Check the filter a week or two after a windy spell, since it often loads up much faster than usual.
faqs: Can pollen grow in my air ducts?
No. Pollen doesn't grow on its own, but it can collect in ducts with other dust. If there's moisture, that buildup can support mold, which is a separate concern.
What filter is best for pollen?
Pleated filters rated MERV 8 to 13 capture pollen well. Higher ratings catch more, but some systems can't handle the extra airflow restriction, so ask a technician what fits yours.
Should I run my HVAC fan to filter out pollen?
Running the fan moves more air through the filter, which can help during allergy season. It does use more electricity, so some people run it in cycles instead of all day.
How do I know if my return ducts are leaking?
Signs include dusty return grilles, dust streaks around the furnace cabinet, a dusty house even with new filters, and rooms that smell like the attic or garage when the system runs.
